doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
title: Non-union rock promoters, Bill Graham and club owners
summary: Teen dances and rock promoters undercut union musicians and club owners start hiring singing groups.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: door and they got eight hundred kids, see I know over at the Lake Marriott Hotel, no not the Lake Marriott the – oh it wasn’t the Lake Marriott, because they didn’t have the public dances there — the Leamington Hotel in Oakland, they had a ballroom and the guys would promote dances. And we used to get calls from the management, “We’d like to know if you could tell us the band that played there. Our microphone disappeared,” or, “part of our PA system is missing.” Well these were all non-union groups, kids groups. So you know we had no way of knowing but then the Claremont Hotel up there, they decided, they got a young man and they gave him license to have concerts up there for the kids and they would draw, same thing, eight, nine hundred, a thousand people. But the kids, they were kind of rowdy. The cars that were parked, the cars would get trashed and they were just rowdy and the guests complained so they stopped that after a while. But in the meantime that was non-union activity, so that means that the union musicians don’t get the gig, and then Bill Graham, he’d come into town and he started promoting over at the Fillmore auditorium. So he would do the same thing. He’d have a garage band. They’d have a lesser name plus a garage band. And $75 — “After all, man, you’re getting a chance for exposure — exposure. This job is going to lead to” so and so. But then he’d have a semi-name, and then later he moved into Winterland. Then he started that, because they had a larger capacity. And then he became really big. And of course he opened up the thing down at I guess it’s Shoreline, wherever that is down in Mountain View, that’s really a big thing. But what it did, the club owners then suddenly they wanted singing groups and then with the rock & roll you’d have two guitars, electric bass, drums, and if they had a tenor player you’d have a guy, you had a tenor player sometimes, and what they would play, it was very, very loud music with a very simple harmonics structure, maybe three chords. So the club owners they just started hiring singing groups and those rhythm & blues and rock & roll groups. And for jazz it just pushed us out of the picture. And many of the big bands, they disbanded. Even Duke’s band, there was an exodus out of his band with Johnny Hodges and Lawrence Brown and all those guys and they went out with Norman Granz. They had “Castle Rock.” They had a hit record called “Castle Rock.” See but they had left him. That band, they played the Black Hawk. Sonny Greer wasn’t with them but the Lawrence Brown and Hodges, and I think Rudy Williams was on clarinet. And I don’t know the bass player, drummer and piano. And Basie. Remember Basie had the small group?
